title: The Importance of Rehearsal When Coaching
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton reflects on how he came round to rehearsal as a step in instructional coaching. Having long found it awkward and rushed it, or skipped it, he now treats it as essential after a two-day coach-training event where he saw three rehearsals expose gaps that discussion had missed. In one a teacher abandoned his planned response to a wrong mini-whiteboard answer mid-way, in another a teacher cold called individuals when practising Call and Respond, and in a third a What if? sequence made too large a jump. The lesson is that there is a gulf between thinking about a teaching move and enacting it, partly down to the Curse of Knowledge. Teachers resist rehearsal because it feels weird and because they believe they do not need it, so coaches should make it low-stakes and explain its purpose, ideally with more than one person in the room. Coachees should embrace it as a step toward classroom enactment.
points: Barton admits his earlier coaching was vague and that he rushed or skipped rehearsal because it felt awkward, which made it ineffective for the coaches he led.
Three live examples (Book-to-Board, Call and Respond, What If) each revealed a flaw that was invisible during the planning conversation.
There is a gap between visualising a technique and performing it, and the Curse of Knowledge makes coaches underestimate its nuances.
Teachers resist rehearsal because it is awkward and because they assume they are ready, so coaches must build safe, low-stakes conditions and explain the point.
Group coaching with more than one adult can make rehearsal feel more natural.
quotes: I would wander into a classroom with no real purpose, watch teachers teach thinking “well, I wouldn’t have done that”, and give vague feedback along the lines of “I think you need to work on your differentiation”.

The thing is, I know it is important for teachers to have an opportunity to rehearse the idea we have just discussed and planned during the coaching conversation. But it has always felt weird to me, and hence, I made it feel weird to my coaches.
One of the coaches had deliberately made an error to give the teacher an opportunity to practice how he would respond to this scenario.

At the end of this, I thanked him for his enthusiasm and clear delivery, and then said that I would give it a go so I could model what I actually meant. Immediately he said: Sorry, I see it now, and was able to do the action again but this time involving all of us.
The jump between the 3rd and 4th examples was too big. Too many things are changing.
The key point from each of these examples is that there is a gulf between thinking about a teaching move and enacting one. This may come down to the Curse of Knowledge.
You don’t want the first time you try to put something new into practice to be in front of 30 expectant pairs of eyes with a million other things vying for your attention.
